EU-ForDAM: correlation metrics, insect vs insect

Does damage from different agents fluctuate together? (basis for objectives 1-3)

Published

October 13, 2026

Why

The thesis rests on one premise: damage from different agents tends to fluctuate together, so the existing records carry information about the missing ones. This section tests that premise directly, for every pair of insect codes in EU-ForDAM.

How

  • Pairs: all 49 insect codes as reported (species, genus codes and aggregate groups), 1,176 pairs.
  • Data: value1; 0 = monitored, no damage; empty = not monitored. Only region-years where both codes are recorded.
  • Scale: log(1 + damage), each region’s series measured against its own mean, so large and small regions are comparable.
  • Measure: Pearson r (−1 = opposite, 0 = no link, +1 = always together), with a 95% range from resampling whole regions 999 times. A link is clear when the range excludes 0.

Five questions per pair:

Question Metric
Q1 Do they have bad years together? same-year r
Q2 Still linked after removing Europe-wide bad years? r after removing each code’s Europe-wide yearly mean
Q3 Does one come first? A in year t vs B in year t+1, beyond B’s own persistence
Q4 Does the link hold in each country? r per country; consistent = same sign, similar size, no country flips it
Q5 Do linked insects share a broad group or host tree? mean r by shared group vs 999 random relabellings

Q1 and Q2: which insects fluctuate together?

link pairs share
strong, beyond shared bad years 74 6%
strong, mostly shared bad years 32 3%
weak but real 123 10%
no clear link 778 66%
not enough data 169 14%
  • 1007 pairs can be measured; 229 have a clear link.
  • 74 pairs are strongly linked even after removing Europe-wide bad years (Q2): their link is not just shared weather.
  • The links concentrate in the borers on conifers block (top left of the matrix). Borers on broadleaves also link to them; defoliators link mainly among themselves; borers and defoliators rarely link.
  • A few clear negative links (blue): e.g. Pristiphora abietina with the spruce bark-borer group and I. duplicatus (one high when the other is low).

Most connected insects (number of strong links beyond shared bad years): ips_cem (12), pis_pin (11), tom_spp (10), pit_cha (9), pha_cya (9), ips_acu (9).

Q3: does one come first?

Of 1,937 directional tests (A this year, B next year), 215 are clear, about 2.2 times the 97 expected by chance. Lead effects exist but are weaker and less certain than same-year links; most involve few regions (5-10). Strongest: sco_int then pit_bid; xyl_lin then xyl_spp; sco_int then pis_pin. Full list: outputs/tables/CM_basic_Q3_lead_effects.csv.

Q4: does a link hold across countries?

Q4_holds_across_countries strong pairs share
consistent 30 28%
inconsistent 19 18%
insufficient data 57 54%

Of the 106 strong pairs, 30 hold consistently in every country where they can be checked, 19 differ between countries, and 57 are recorded together in fewer than two countries, so this cannot be checked. This matters for gap-filling, which uses links learnt in one country to fill another. Example of a consistent link: I. typographus with Pityokteines spp. (AT, DE, HR, SI); example of an inconsistent one: I. typographus with Pityogenes chalcographus (strong in DE, AT, SI; near zero or negative in LT, SK, IT).

Q5: do the links follow host trees and feeding type?

metric pairs that share n_pairs mean_r mean r, random labels p_value
same year different broad groups 702 0.07 0.08 0.994
same year same broad group only (level 1) 162 0.16 0.08 0.002
same year same host-tree group (level 2) 143 0.08 0.08 0.623
beyond shared bad years different broad groups 673 0.07 0.08 0.952
beyond shared bad years same broad group only (level 1) 162 0.10 0.07 0.140
beyond shared bad years same host-tree group (level 2) 134 0.09 0.08 0.100

Insects in the same broad group (borers / defoliators on conifers / broadleaves) have bad years together more than chance (p = 0.002). Sharing the same host tree adds nothing beyond that. After removing Europe-wide bad years, no grouping clearly beats chance.

What it means for the thesis

  1. The premise holds, partly. About a fifth of measurable pairs are clearly linked, strongest among bark and wood borers on conifers. These insects carry information about each other; most other pairs do not.
  2. Most strong links are more than shared bad years (Q1 vs Q2): 74 of 106 strong pairs stay linked after removing Europe-wide bad years; the other 32 are mainly years that were bad everywhere. Shared drivers (drought, storms) acting regionally are a likely source; adding those data later should explain part of the links (objective 3).
  3. Transfer between countries is the limiting factor. Many strong links cannot be checked in a second country; where they can, about 6 in 10 hold. Gap-filling should rely most on consistent links (objective 1).
  4. Feeding type matters more than host tree: borers move with borers, defoliators with defoliators.
